foreign_collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (1994.420)
angle: Two artists reimagine a real mountain through different painting traditions.
similarities: Both paintings depict recognizable mountains: Mount Inwang in Korea and Mont Sainte-Victoire in southern France.|Both artists were familiar with their subjects: Jeong Seon lived near Mount Inwang, while Cézanne repeatedly studied Mont Sainte-Victoire near Aix-en-Provence.|Both transform observed landscapes through deliberate pictorial choices rather than simply recording geographical features.
differences: Jeong Seon builds the rain-soaked mass of Mount Inwang, especially Chimabawi, with dense dark ink strokes; Cézanne constructs mountain and terrain through layered oil brushstrokes and color relationships.|Jeong Seon leaves paper unpainted and applies pale washes to evoke mist between rocky peaks; Cézanne organizes land, trees, mountain, and sky through interacting areas of color.|Jeong Seon combines an elevated view of foreground buildings with an upward view of towering peaks; Cézanne emphasizes relationships among forms and colors within a broad landscape.|Jeong Seon includes pines and small buildings to establish scale; Cézanne presents a wider panorama on a canvas he expanded during its creation.|Cézanne painted Mont Sainte-Victoire repeatedly over decades; an equivalent repeated process is not documented for Inwangjesaekdo.
source_note: [AI 도슨트 운영 메모] 두 작품 모두 실제 산을 회화적으로 재구성한다는 점은 비교 해석이다. 두 화가 사이의 직접적인 영향 관계는 확인되지 않는다. 세잔의 반복 제작과 캔버스 확장 과정을 정선에게 적용하지 않는다.
foreign_key_facts: Paul Cézanne painted Mont Sainte-Victoire around 1902–1906, using oil paint on canvas.|Mont Sainte-Victoire is a mountain near Aix-en-Provence in southern France, where Cézanne was born and raised.|Cézanne depicted this mountain dozens of times over several decades, exploring different views and compositions.|Cézanne initially placed the mountain near the center, then expanded the canvas to the right and bottom, transforming the composition into a broader panorama.|Cézanne used small, often parallel brushstrokes and interrelated areas of color to construct the land, trees, mountain, and sky without relying solely on traditional linear perspective.|Cézanne studied the natural structure of landscapes around Aix, including their geological formations.|His approach to constructing forms through color became influential in the development of modern painting, including Cubism.
foreign_source_note: The Met 작품 페이지(1994.420)에서 작가, 제작 시기, 재료, 소장 정보 확인. The Met 소장품 도록 《Recent Acquisitions 1994–1995》에서 캔버스 확장 과정 확인. The Met 세잔 해설과 NGA 교육 자료에서 생트빅투아르산의 반복 제작, 색채·붓질 및 풍경 연구의 특징 참고.

foreign_title: South Wind, Clear Sky (Gaifū kaisei), also known as Red Fuji, from the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji
foreign_collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (JP9)
angle: Two iconic mountains transformed by contrasting atmospheric conditions and artistic techniques.
similarities: Both works make a recognizable mountain their dominant subject: Mount Inwang in Korea and Mount Fuji in Japan.|Both use contrasting areas to evoke atmospheric conditions: Jeong Seon depicts rain-darkened rocks emerging from mist, while Hokusai sets a red mountain against a clear blue sky.|Both simplify or reorganize aspects of real geography to create a striking image rather than a strictly literal topographical record.
differences: Jeong Seon depicts the rugged, rain-soaked Chimabawi rocks with layered dark ink; Hokusai defines Mount Fuji through broad red slopes and sharply contrasting printed colors.|Jeong Seon uses blank paper and pale ink washes for mist; Hokusai contrasts the red mountain with blue sky, pale clouds, and green foothills.|Jeong Seon includes pines, trees, and partly hidden buildings in the foreground; Hokusai omits buildings and figures and reduces trees to tiny shapes near the mountain’s base.|Jeong Seon combines different viewpoints to heighten Mount Inwang’s scale; Hokusai emphasizes Mount Fuji’s simplified silhouette.|Inwangjesaekdo is an individual ink painting on paper; Red Fuji is a multicolored woodblock print from the Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji series, surviving in multiple impressions.
source_note: [AI 도슨트 운영 메모] 두 작품의 날씨와 산의 표현 방식에 관한 비교는 해석적 관점이며 직접적인 영향 관계는 확인되지 않는다. 붉은 후지산을 특정 날짜의 실제 풍경으로 단정하지 않고, 같은 판화의 여러 인쇄본을 서로 다른 작품으로 설명하지 않는다.
foreign_key_facts: Hokusai’s South Wind, Clear Sky, also known as Red Fuji, belongs to his Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji series, produced around 1830–1832.|The series explores Mount Fuji from different viewpoints and under changing atmospheric conditions.|The mountain’s reddish color is traditionally associated with dawn in early autumn, although the print does not document a specific observed morning.|Mount Fuji dominates the composition without people or buildings; small green triangular shapes representing trees along its base emphasize its immense scale.|The mountain’s red slopes contrast with the blue sky, pale clouds, and green foothills, while the simplified silhouette and patterned clouds give the image a striking graphic quality.|The image was produced as a multicolored woodblock print, using ink and color on paper rather than being painted as a unique original.|The series was expanded from its original thirty-six designs to forty-six after its commercial success.|Multiple impressions of Red Fuji survive; The Metropolitan Museum of Art holds examples of the same design under different accession numbers.
foreign_source_note: The Met 작품 페이지 및 Collection API(36490, 55736, 57007)에서 작품명, 연대, 재료와 동일 디자인의 여러 인쇄본 확인. The Met 소장품 해설에서 초가을 새벽의 붉은 후지산, 인물 없는 구성, 작은 나무와 구름의 표현 확인. The Met의 《후가쿠 36경》 관련 해설에서 다양한 기상·시점과 연작 확장 내용 참고.
korean_source_note: e뮤지엄 《인왕제색도》 소장품 정보와 국립중앙박물관 작품 해설에서 비 갠 인왕산의 먹과 안개 표현, 전경 구성 및 진경산수화의 특징 참고.

angle: Everyday gatherings transformed into carefully composed scenes.
similarities: Both paintings make communal activities their subject: spectators gather around a wrestling match in Joseon Korea, while guests attend a rural wedding feast in sixteenth-century Flanders.|Both artists arrange groups of people and ordinary objects to make a lively gathering visually coherent.|Both reward close observation of varied gestures and reactions, from wrestling spectators to wedding guests, musicians, and food servers.
differences: Kim Hong-do centers two wrestlers within a roughly circular group of spectators against a largely empty background; Bruegel fills an interior with a long banquet table and numerous guests.|In Ssireum, a toffee vendor and pairs of shoes balance the circular arrangement; in Peasant Wedding, the table and movement of food servers organize the crowded room.|Kim captures the unresolved tension of a single wrestling exchange, including one competitor lifting a leg; Bruegel shows several activities unfolding during a wedding feast.|Kim uses economical brushwork and expressive faces on a small paper album leaf; Bruegel uses detailed oil painting on a much larger oak panel.|Ssireum does not establish the specific festival or occasion of its contest; Peasant Wedding explicitly depicts a wedding celebration.
source_note: [AI 도슨트 운영 메모] 두 작품의 군중 구성과 일상생활 묘사에 관한 공통점은 비교 해석이며 직접적인 영향 관계는 확인되지 않는다. 브뤼헐 작품의 풍자적·도덕적 의도는 확정되지 않았으므로 단정하지 않는다. 두 작품의 인물들을 동일한 사회계층이나 문화적 관습으로 일반화하지 않는다.
foreign_key_facts: Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted Peasant Wedding around 1567–1568, depicting a rural wedding feast in sixteenth-century Flanders.|The celebration takes place in a barn-like interior, with guests seated along a long table and others standing or moving around them.|The bride sits in front of a green hanging, with a paper wedding crown suspended above her head.|According to the Kunsthistorisches Museum’s discussion of Flemish wedding customs, the bridegroom was not seated at the wedding table; the painting does not securely identify him.|Two servers carry bowls of food on a wooden door removed from its hinges and repurposed as a large serving tray.|At the left, a man pours drink into jugs, while musicians and other guests contribute to the lively atmosphere.|The painting includes figures identified in the museum’s description as a lawyer, a Franciscan monk, and the lord of the manor accompanied by a dog.|Although the celebration appears spontaneous, Bruegel carefully arranges the long table, food servers, and standing guests to guide the viewer through the crowded interior.|Bruegel depicts ordinary rural life through detailed gestures, clothing, food, and social interactions rather than focusing on rulers or mythological figures.|The painting is executed in oil on an oak panel, allowing detailed representation of figures, clothing, and objects across a large surface.|Scholars have debated whether the painting contains satire or a moral lesson, but its precise intended meaning remains uncertain.
foreign_source_note: Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien 작품 페이지(GG 1027)와 KHM 공식 도록 해설에서 혼인 잔치의 구성, 신부와 하객, 음식 운반 장면, 당시 풍습 및 작품 해석의 논쟁 확인. Getty CONA에서 작품 식별정보, 재료, 소장번호와 1568년경 연대 확인. KHM 2018년 브뤼헐 전시 자료에는 1567년경으로 표기되어 연대 자료 간 차이가 있음.
korean_source_note: e뮤지엄 《씨름》 소장품 정보 및 국립중앙박물관 작품 해설에서 씨름꾼과 관중의 원형 구도, 엿장수와 신발의 구성상 역할, 인물의 표정과 붓질 표현 확인.

angle: Children's learning and play seen through two contrasting compositions.
similarities: Both paintings portray children through varied actions, gestures, and responses rather than treating them as anonymous figures.|Both organize multiple figures to make everyday social interactions legible, from classmates reacting to a crying pupil to children engaged in games and imitations of adult activities.|Both invite viewers to discover small details within the scene, although the number of figures and spatial scale differ greatly.
differences: Kim Hong-do concentrates on a single classroom episode involving a crying pupil, teacher, and classmates; Bruegel spreads many games across a town square and adjoining streets.|Kim arranges the figures in a compact circle against an almost empty background; Bruegel uses an elevated viewpoint and receding streets to organize a large, densely populated setting.|Kim uses concise brushwork to distinguish individual expressions; Bruegel employs detailed oil painting to describe many small figures, objects, and activities.|Seodang depicts a Joseon school setting associated with classical recitation and historical disciplinary practices; Children’s Games depicts recreation, including children imitating adult roles.|The suggestion that the crying pupil was punished after failing a recitation assessment remains an interpretation; Bruegel’s possible moral or educational intentions are also debated.
source_note: [AI 도슨트 운영 메모] 두 작품을 어린이의 사회적 활동이라는 관점에서 비교하는 것은 해석적 접근이며, 직접적인 영향 관계는 확인되지 않는다. 《서당》의 교육 장면과 《아이들의 놀이》의 놀이 장면을 동일한 교육 방식으로 설명하지 않는다. 브뤼헐 작품의 풍자적·도덕적 의미나 교육적 의도를 확정된 사실로 단정하지 않는다. 놀이의 종류와 인물 수는 자료별 집계 차이를 고려한다.
foreign_key_facts: Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted Children’s Games in 1560, using oil paint on an oak panel.|The painting depicts a large town square and adjoining streets filled with approximately 230 figures, most of them children, engaged in numerous activities.|More than eighty different games and playful activities can be identified, although published counts vary.|Bruegel uses a high, bird’s-eye viewpoint to make many small scenes visible; a street on the right recedes toward the city center while the left background opens toward a village and rural landscape.|Children play with hoops, tops, stilts, and other objects, while some take part in games that remain familiar today.|Some children imitate adult activities, including wedding ceremonies, christenings, and shopkeeping.|The figures display a wide range of behaviors and emotions, from quiet play to aggressive interactions.|The composition is often described as a Wimmelbild, a densely populated picture filled with numerous small scenes.|Bruegel signed and dated the painting BRVEGEL 1560 on a beam near the lower right of the composition.|The painting has been interpreted both as a survey of children’s games and as possible commentary on human behavior, but its intended message remains debated.|Art historian Amy Orrock has explored the painting in relation to sixteenth-century humanist educational ideas, offering a scholarly interpretation rather than proof of Bruegel’s intentions.
foreign_source_note: KHM 작품 해설 및 2010년 도록에서 높은 시점의 구도, 도시·시골 공간, 230명 이상의 인물과 83가지 놀이 확인. KHM 브뤼헐 특별전 자료에서 서명·제작 연도, 어른의 행동을 모방하는 놀이, 다양한 감정 표현 및 90가지 이상이라는 다른 집계 확인. Amy Orrock의 JHNA 논문에서 16세기 인문주의 교육 사상과 관련한 학술적 해석 참고.
korean_source_note: e뮤지엄 《서당》 소장품 정보와 국립중앙박물관 작품 해설 및 작품 이미지에서 훈장과 학생들의 배치, 우는 아이와 주변 학생들의 반응, 배경을 생략한 구도와 간결한 붓질 표현 참고.

foreign_title: Hokusai Sketchbooks (Denshin kaishu: Hokusai manga), first volume
foreign_collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (JIB81.1)
angle: Human movement and physical encounters depicted through expressive drawing in two different artistic traditions.
similarities: Both works portray physical encounters through expressive bodily gestures: Kim Hong-do depicts a wrestling match, while an illustration documented in the first volume of Hokusai Manga depicts a street brawl.|Both use economical lines and varied poses to convey movement without elaborate modeling of the figures.|Both invite attention to how people interact, from the wrestlers and their spectators to the figures involved in the illustrated brawl.
differences: Kim depicts an organized wrestling match between two competitors; Hokusai’s identified illustration depicts a street brawl involving several figures, not a formal contest.|Kim centers the wrestlers within a roughly circular arrangement of spectators; Hokusai distributes the moving figures across an open setting with buildings in the background.|Kim uses a toffee vendor and pairs of shoes to balance the composition; Hokusai includes architecture and people engaged in different actions.|Kim uses expressive brushwork and a largely empty background to focus on one unresolved moment; Hokusai uses printed linework to show simultaneous movements.|Ssireum is a unique painted album leaf; Hokusai Manga is a woodblock-printed illustrated book containing diverse subjects and existing in multiple impressions.
source_note: [AI 도슨트 운영 메모] 두 작품의 신체 움직임과 인물 표현에 관한 유사점은 비교 해석이며 직접적인 영향 관계는 확인되지 않는다. 김홍도의 《씨름》은 경기 장면이고 호쿠사이의 삽화는 거리의 몸싸움 장면이므로 동일한 경기나 사회적 관습으로 설명하지 않는다. NGV 등 다른 소장본에서 확인한 몸싸움 삽화가 The Met의 JIB81.1에도 수록되었는지는 직접 대조되지 않았다. 따라서 verified는 제1권 단위의 작품 정보와 비교 근거에 대한 검증을 뜻하며, JIB81.1의 특정 페이지까지 확인했다는 뜻은 아니다. 씨름 경기의 승패나 특정 명절을 단정하지 않는다. 제1권의 1814년 최초 출판과 Met 소장본의 1828년 이후 연대를 구분한다.
foreign_key_facts: Hokusai Manga is a series of woodblock-printed illustrated books by Katsushika Hokusai, depicting human figures, animals, plants, landscapes, historical subjects, and supernatural themes.|The first volume was originally published in 1814, whereas The Metropolitan Museum of Art dates its particular first-volume copy, JIB81.1, to after 1828.|The Met’s first-volume copy is printed with ink and color on paper and measures approximately 22.9 × 15.9 × 1 cm.|Hokusai’s sketches capture characteristic human poses, actions, and bodily movement through economical, expressive drawing.|The images were reproduced using woodblocks, distinguishing the published books from unique, individually painted artworks.|The series eventually comprised fifteen volumes: the first ten appeared between 1814 and 1819, and additional volumes were published over subsequent decades, including after Hokusai’s death in 1849.|The term manga in the title referred to miscellaneous or informal sketches and should not be equated directly with the narrative format of modern Japanese comics.|An illustration associated with the first volume depicts several figures in a street brawl; this scene is documented in National Gallery of Victoria exhibition materials, but its presence in The Met’s JIB81.1 copy has not been directly checked.
foreign_source_note: The Met 작품 페이지 및 Collection API(objects/57679)에서 제1권 소장본 JIB81.1의 제목, 1828년 이후 연대, 목판 인쇄본의 재료와 크기 확인. The Met 《Random Sketches by Hokusai, Volumes 1 to 11》(JIB111a–k) 해설에서 인체 움직임 표현, 1814년 최초 출판 및 15권으로 확장된 연작의 역사 확인. The Met 공식 도록 《Hokusai》(1985)에서 인물·동물·식물·풍경 등 다양한 소재와 목판 인쇄 제작 과정 참고. British Museum의 호쿠사이 전시 자료에서 manga의 의미와 출판 역사 교차 확인.
korean_source_note: 최종 artworks.csv의 KHD_SSIREUM key_facts를 기준으로 e뮤지엄·국립중앙박물관에서 씨름꾼의 움직임, 관중의 원형 구도, 엿장수와 신발의 구성상 역할, 인물의 표정과 간결한 붓질 확인. 국립민속박물관 한국민속대백과사전에서 씨름의 역사와 경기 방식 참고.

angle: Two artists construct their identities through self-portraiture, clothing, and written inscriptions.
similarities: Both portraits present an artist’s likeness as a statement of identity, although Kang Se-hwang’s traditional attribution as a self-portrait has been questioned.|Both use clothing to shape the sitter’s public image: Dürer wears a fur-trimmed robe, while Kang combines an official hat with informal scholar’s robes.|Both include inscriptions that connect the sitter to a personal identity: Dürer names himself and his age, while Kang reflects on his learning, art, and life between court and retreat.
differences: Dürer faces the viewer frontally in a close half-length portrait; Kang appears seated in a full-length composition with his face slightly turned.|The Alte Pinakothek relates Dürer’s frontal pose and hand gesture to images of Christ the Saviour; Kang’s combination of official hat and informal robes is interpreted through his inscription as expressing public service and scholarly retreat.|Dürer shows long hair, fur-trimmed clothing, and a visible hand against a dark background; Kang wears pale jade-blue robes and a red belt, with his hands concealed in wide sleeves.|Dürer’s Latin inscription identifies him as twenty-eight in 1500; Kang’s inscription records his age as seventy by traditional Korean reckoning in 1782.|Dürer models his features in oil on a linden-wood panel; Kang uses fine lines and subtle shading in ink and color on silk.
source_note: [AI 도슨트 운영 메모] 두 화가의 자화상을 통한 정체성 표현은 비교 해석이며 직접적인 영향 관계는 확인되지 않는다. 뒤러의 그리스도 성상과의 시각적 연관성은 공식 미술관 해설에 근거하지만 자신을 그리스도와 동일시하려 했다는 제작 의도로 확대하지 않는다. 강세황의 자화상은 전통적으로 1782년 작품으로 알려져 있으나 작가 귀속에 관한 이견이 있음을 고려한다. 강세황의 관모와 야복의 의미는 자찬문과 공식 해설을 근거로 설명한다. 1782년 자화상과 다른 강세황 초상, 특히 덕수 3069를 혼동하지 않는다.
foreign_key_facts: Albrecht Dürer painted Self-Portrait with Fur-Trimmed Robe in 1500, when he was twenty-eight years old.|The painting belongs to the Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen and is housed in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich under inventory number 537.|The portrait is painted in oil on a linden wood panel measuring 67.1 × 48.9 cm.|Dürer presents himself in a direct frontal pose, with symmetrical long hair, detailed facial features, and a fur-trimmed robe against a dark background.|According to the Alte Pinakothek, Dürer drew on the visual conventions of images of Christ the Saviour, particularly the frontal pose and gesture of the hand.|The sitter’s direct gaze and carefully depicted hand are interpreted by the museum as referring to seeing and artistic creation.|The painting includes a Latin inscription identifying Dürer as an artist from Nuremberg who portrayed himself at the age of twenty-eight.|Dürer’s distinctive monogram and the date 1500 appear on the painting.|The Alte Pinakothek acquired the painting from Nuremberg in 1805.
foreign_source_note: Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Alte Pinakothek 공식 작품 페이지(Self-Portrait with Fur-Trimmed Robe, Inv. 537)에서 작품명, 작가, 1500년 연대, 린덴나무 패널, 크기, 소장번호, 1805년 구입 기록 확인. 공식 해설에서 라틴어 명문, 정면 구도, 구세주 그리스도 성상의 도상적 참조 및 시선과 손의 표현에 관한 해석 확인. 알테 피나코테크가 Google Arts & Culture에 제공한 작품 해설과 Smarthistory의 작품 분석을 보조 자료로 참고.
korean_source_note: 최종 artworks.csv의 KSH_SELF key_facts를 기준으로 국가유산 지식이음의 강세황 자화상(1782) 해설에서 70세 자화상이라는 전통적 식별, 오사모와 야복의 조합, 옥빛 옷과 붉은 띠, 자찬문의 내용 및 얼굴의 세부 표현 확인. e뮤지엄과 국가유산 관련 자료에서 작품 기본정보와 작가 생애 참고. 국립중앙박물관의 별도 강세황 초상(덕수 3069)과 구분.

foreign_title: Self Portrait at the Age of 63
angle: Two artists explore ageing and self-representation through contrasting approaches to portraiture.
similarities: Both works are identified as self-portraits made late in the sitters’ lives, although Kang Se-hwang’s attribution remains debated: Rembrandt was sixty-three in 1669, and Kang’s inscription gives his age as seventy by traditional Korean reckoning in 1782.|Both portraits give close attention to signs of ageing, including facial wrinkles and changes in facial contours.|Both use tonal variation to model an individual face, despite working in different media and portrait traditions.
differences: Rembrandt emphasizes his illuminated face in a relatively close composition against a dark background; Kang presents himself seated full-length in official headwear and informal robes.|Rembrandt uses thick oil paint, translucent layers, and contrasting light to render ageing skin; Kang describes wrinkles with fine lines and subtle shading on silk.|Rembrandt paints his clothing and folded hands relatively loosely; Kang’s concealed hands, pale jade-blue robes, and red belt contribute to a carefully arranged full-length image.|X-ray examination suggests that Rembrandt initially painted himself holding a brush before revising the composition; Kang’s portrait includes an inscription describing his learning, artistic identity, and position between court and retreat.|Rembrandt painted his work in 1669, the final year of his life; Kang’s portrait is traditionally dated to 1782, with its age recorded in the inscription.|The National Gallery treats interpretations of Rembrandt’s expression as a meditation on death cautiously; Kang’s inscription explicitly discusses his official role and attachment to a scholar’s life.
source_note: [AI 도슨트 운영 메모] 두 작품의 노년과 자기표현에 관한 공통점은 비교 해석이며 직접적인 영향 관계는 확인되지 않는다. 렘브란트가 죽음을 앞두고 자신의 삶을 성찰했다는 해석은 후대의 관점으로, 제작 의도로 단정하지 않는다. 강세황 자화상의 1782년 연대는 자찬문에 근거하며, 김홍도 대필설은 확정된 사실이 아닌 귀속 가설로 취급한다. 렘브란트의 자화상 약 80점과 강세황의 초상 8점을 동일한 기준의 자화상 수량으로 비교하지 않는다. 강세황의 1782년 자화상과 별도 초상인 덕수 3069를 혼동하지 않는다.
foreign_key_facts: Rembrandt painted Self Portrait at the Age of 63 in 1669, the final year of his life; it is one of three self-portraits he made that year.|The painting is held by the National Gallery in London under inventory number NG221.|It is an oil painting on canvas measuring 86 × 70.5 cm.|Approximately eighty self-portraits by Rembrandt survive across paintings, drawings, and prints from his forty-year career.|Rembrandt uses strong illumination to emphasize his ageing face against a comparatively dark background.|He combines thickly applied paint, translucent color layers, and varied hues to depict wrinkles, blemishes, and the textures of ageing skin.|The robe, fur collar, and folded hands are painted more loosely than the face, drawing attention toward his facial features.|X-ray examination revealed that Rembrandt initially depicted himself with what appears to be a brush in his hand before altering the composition.|Although later writers have interpreted the painting as self-examination in the face of death, the National Gallery notes that Rembrandt may also have been exploring the technical challenges of depicting ageing skin.
foreign_source_note: National Gallery 공식 작품 페이지(Self Portrait at the Age of 63, NG221)에서 작품명, 작가, 1669년 연대, 유채·캔버스 재료, 크기 및 소장번호 확인. 작품 해설에서 렘브란트의 자화상 제작 역사, 노년의 얼굴에 대한 관심, 두꺼운 물감과 반투명 색층의 사용, 옷과 배경의 간략한 표현 및 X선 조사로 확인된 구도 수정 참고. National Gallery 공식 소장품 도록(The Dutch School, 1600–1900)에서 서명·연대와 물감층의 두께 및 표면 질감 확인. 죽음을 앞둔 자기성찰이라는 해석은 확정된 제작 의도가 아니라 후대의 해석으로 구분.
